t: SQL Training Guide — Oracle SQL Developer for HR Systems
s: A comprehensive reference guide for querying PeopleXD using Oracle SQL Developer. Covers SELECT statements, WHERE clauses, JOINs, aggregation, and Oxford HR-specific context. Suitable for beginners and as an ongoing reference.
_text:
SQL Training Guide — Oracle SQL Developer for HR Systems

Purpose

This guide covers how to query the PeopleXD (CoreHR) database using Oracle SQL Developer. All access is read-only — you cannot change, delete, or break any data in PeopleXD. This is a safe environment to learn and experiment.

SQL Dialects — Important

There are different types of SQL. At Oxford HR Systems, we use two:

Oracle PL/SQL — used in SQL Developer to query the PeopleXD database directly. This is what this guide covers.

TSQL (Transact-SQL) — used in Visual Studio when editing .RDL report files. Broadly similar to Oracle SQL but has syntax differences. If you copy SQL from one environment to the other, it may need adjustments.

When searching online for SQL help, always specify which dialect you are using (e.g. search "Oracle SQL GROUP BY" not just "SQL GROUP BY"). MySQL, PostgreSQL and other dialects also exist but are not used in this role.

Connecting to the Database

When you open SQL Developer you will see a list of saved connections on the left-hand panel. Each connection represents a different database or environment (e.g. UOXZ for the Z environment). Once you have connected to a database, any query window you open will run against that database. The connection name is shown at the top of each query window so you always know which environment you are querying.

The database objects panel (left side) shows Tables, Views, and Functions available to your connection. The HR data we work with is owned by the core HR user, which owns the BI layer — the views we query sit within this schema.

Always use Views, not Tables

By agreement with the Access Group, HR Systems queries data from views rather than tables directly. Views are pre-built by the Access Group and give you clean, reliable fields. You will see tables listed in SQL Developer but you should not query these directly unless you have a specific reason and are confident in what you are doing.

Common views you will encounter:

PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER — person-level data including forename, surname, person reference, pay group, employment status.

Appointment history views — appointment-level data including appointment ID, start dates, status.

Functions also exist in the database (Oracle built-in functions and custom Access Group functions). These are used for things like pulling UDF (User Defined Field) information and salary data. You will encounter them when reading existing SQL scripts. They appear as function names followed by brackets containing parameters.

Basic SELECT Statement

The simplest SQL query selects data from a view or table.

Syntax:
SELECT column1, column2 FROM view_name

Example:
SELECT forename, surname FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER

This returns every person's forename and surname from the entire database. Separate column names with commas. You can select as many columns as you need.

Using a WHERE Clause

A WHERE clause filters the results. Add it after the FROM clause.

Syntax:
SELECT column1, column2 FROM view_name WHERE condition

Example — filter to active employees only:
SELECT forename, surname FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER WHERE employment_status = 'S'

Employment status 'S' means active (commenced) in PeopleXD. Most queries should include this filter to exclude dormant and historical records.

WHERE Clause Operators

You can use a range of operators in WHERE clauses:

= (equals) — exact match. String values need single quotes; numeric values do not.
Example: WHERE forename = 'Sarah'

!= or <> (not equals) — excludes a specific value.
Example: WHERE employment_status != 'S'

> < >= <= — greater than, less than, etc. Useful for dates and numbers.

IN() — matches any value in a list. String values need single quotes; numeric values do not.
Example: WHERE pay_group IN (10, 20, 30)
Example: WHERE surname IN ('Smith', 'Jones')

NOT IN() — excludes all values in the list.
Example: WHERE pay_code NOT IN (100, 105)

BETWEEN — matches values within a range (inclusive). Good for dates and numbers.
Example: WHERE start_date BETWEEN '01-JAN-2025' AND '31-DEC-2025'

LIKE — pattern matching using wildcards. Requires single quotes.
% at the start means ends with: WHERE surname LIKE '%ton' (returns Preston, Morton, Thurston etc.)
% at the end means starts with: WHERE surname LIKE 'Smi%'
% at both ends means contains: WHERE view_name LIKE '%pay%calendar%'

NOT LIKE — opposite of LIKE.

IS NULL — finds records with no value in that field.
IS NOT NULL — finds records that do have a value.

Combining Conditions

Use AND, OR, and NOT to combine multiple WHERE conditions.

Example:
SELECT forename, surname FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
WHERE employment_status = 'S'
AND surname LIKE '%ton'

If you have a syntax error (pink wiggly underline in SQL Developer), check that you have used AND, OR, or NOT between each condition. Missing an operator is one of the most common errors.

ORDER BY

Add ORDER BY at the end of your query to sort results.

Syntax:
SELECT column1 FROM view_name ORDER BY column1

Default sort is ascending (A to Z, 0 to highest). To sort descending, add DESC:
ORDER BY surname DESC

Column Aliasing

You can rename columns in your results using AS (the alias keyword). This is useful when column names are long or when you are using aggregation functions.

Example:
SELECT COUNT(person_reference) AS number_of_people FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER

You can also omit AS and just put the alias name after the column — Oracle accepts both:
SELECT COUNT(person_reference) number_of_people FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER

Note: do not use reserved words like GROUP as an alias — Oracle will reject it.

Commenting Out Code

Two dashes (--) comment out everything after them on that line. The query engine ignores commented text.

Uses:
1. Soft-delete a line without removing it — useful when testing different versions of a query.
2. Add explanatory notes to your SQL that other people can read.

Example:
SELECT forename, surname FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
WHERE employment_status = 'S' -- active employees only
-- AND pay_group = 10 -- temporarily removed for testing

Aggregation and GROUP BY

Aggregation functions perform calculations across multiple rows. The most common ones are:

COUNT() — counts the number of rows.
SUM() — adds up numeric values.
MAX() — returns the highest value.
MIN() — returns the lowest value.

When you use an aggregation function, every other column in your SELECT must appear in a GROUP BY clause. GROUP BY goes after the WHERE clause.

Example — count people by pay group:
SELECT pay_group, COUNT(person_reference) AS headcount
FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
WHERE employment_status = 'S'
GROUP BY pay_group
ORDER BY pay_group

HAVING Clause

HAVING filters results after aggregation has been applied, whereas WHERE filters before aggregation. HAVING goes after GROUP BY.

Example — only show pay groups with more than 50 active employees:
SELECT pay_group, COUNT(person_reference) AS headcount
FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER
WHERE employment_status = 'S'
GROUP BY pay_group
HAVING COUNT(person_reference) > 50

JOINs

Joins combine data from two or more tables or views. Modern syntax uses JOIN in the FROM section rather than the old-style plus signs in the WHERE clause (you may see the old syntax in legacy SQL — do not write it, but be aware it exists).

The three main join types used in HR Systems:

INNER JOIN — returns only rows where there is a match in both tables. Rows with no match are dropped from both sides.

Example:
SELECT pm.forename, pm.surname, ah.appointment_id
FROM PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER pm
INNER JOIN appointment_history ah ON pm.person_reference = ah.person_reference
WHERE pm.employment_status = 'S'

LEFT JOIN — returns all rows from the first (left) table, and matched rows from the second table where they exist. Where there is no match, the second table columns return NULL. This is the most commonly used join type in HR reporting, for example joining to diversity data where not every person has a diversity record.

FULL OUTER JOIN — returns all rows from both tables, matching where possible and returning NULLs where there is no match on either side.

When joining tables, prefix column names with the table or view name (or its alias) followed by a dot, to avoid ambiguity:
pm.person_reference (person_reference from PRBI_HR_PERSON_MASTER aliased as pm)
ah.person_reference (person_reference from appointment_history aliased as ah)

You can add extra conditions to a JOIN clause using AND:
INNER JOIN appointment_history ah ON pm.person_reference = ah.person_reference
AND ah.employment_appointment_status = 'commenced'

Chaining multiple JOINs can cause rows to multiply if the joined table has multiple matching records. Be careful and check row counts as you build complex queries.

Exporting Results

Once your query returns results:
1. Right-click on the results grid.
2. Select Export.
3. Choose CSV format — this is the most reliable option.
4. Do not use INSERT format (this exports as SQL code for importing into another database).
5. Do not use the Excel export — it can miss rows depending on what is highlighted.
6. Browse for a save location, click Next, then Finish.

Debugging Tips

Pink wiggly underline in the editor — syntax error. Hover over it to see the error message. Click the pink bar on the far right of the screen to jump to the error line in a long script.

Toggle line numbers — right-click the script pane and select Toggle Line Numbers. Essential when an error message refers to a specific line number.

Soft-delete with comments — use -- to comment out suspect lines rather than deleting them, so you can restore them easily if needed.

Column count error in GROUP BY — if Oracle says a column is not in the GROUP BY clause, check that every non-aggregated column in your SELECT is listed in the GROUP BY.

t: HOW TO — Add a Pay Code to the HR Report Suite SQL
s: Step-by-step guide for adding a new pay code to the hard-coded pay code filter in the HR Report Suite .RDL files using Visual Studio 2017 via CONNECT Remote Services. Covers the full process from OSM Change Request through to LIVE deployment and sign-off.
_text:
HOW TO — Add a Pay Code to the HR Report Suite SQL

Background

The HR Report Suite contains a set of .RDL (Report Definition Language) files that define the HR reports available to users. Each .RDL file includes an embedded dataset called DataSet1, which contains the main SQL query that drives the report.

Within DataSet1, the SQL includes a hard-coded IN() list of numeric pay codes. This list controls which pay codes are included in the report output. When a new pay code is created in PeopleXD, it will not appear in the HR Report Suite output until it is manually added to this list in each affected .RDL file.

This is a TSQL change (not Oracle PL/SQL). The files are edited in Visual Studio 2017, accessed via CONNECT Remote Services.

Affected report files are typically those in the allowances suite, including PERDEP01 Full Data Set, PERDEP01 Full Data Set with Allowances, and PERDEP20 Approved Allowance Changes, though other files may also be affected depending on the pay code type.

All files in a report suite are versioned together. If you update one file you must increment all files in the suite to the same version number.

Pre-requisites

Before making any change, confirm with Michael or the Access Group that the pay code does exist in PeopleXD and that the omission is a SQL issue (not an Access Group configuration or pay group security issue). This should be verified before raising a Change Request.

Step 1 — Raise an OSM Change Request

Before touching any files, raise a Change Request in OSM (Oxford Service Management):

1. Open OSM and create a new Change Request.
2. Set Category to Report.
3. Set Justification / Type to Bug Fix.
4. Complete all 14 sections using the CR template in the hris-change-requests GitHub repository (templates/change-request-template.md).
5. Submit the CR and note the Change ID number — you will need this to update the Report Summary headers in the .RDL files.
6. Business Owner / Approver is typically Marie Cooksey, Head of HR Systems.

Step 2 — Access Visual Studio via CONNECT Remote Services

1. Open CONNECT Remote Services on your machine (search for it in the Windows Start menu or go to remotedesktop.connect.ox.ac.uk).
2. Click HRIS Reporting - Visual Studio 2017 (the purple icon).
3. When prompted with a security warning about the remote connection from remotedesktop.connect.ox.ac.uk, click Connect.
4. Enter your Oxford SSO username and password when the Windows Security credentials prompt appears.
5. Wait for Visual Studio 2017 to load in the remote session.

Step 3 — Open the TEST Solution

1. In Visual Studio, go to File > Open > Project/Solution.
2. Navigate to the network drive: I:\OUIT\CoreHR Reports
3. Open the solution file (.sln) for the TEST environment.
4. Wait for Solution Explorer to load on the left panel. You will see the .RDL files listed.

Step 4 — Edit DataSet1 in Each Affected .RDL File

Repeat the following for each affected .RDL file:

4a. Double-click the .RDL file in Solution Explorer to open it.

4b. Find DataSet1. In the report design view, locate the dataset named DataSet1. Right-click it and select Edit Query (or similar) to open the SQL editor.

4c. Find the pay code IN() list. Look in the WHERE clause for a list of numeric pay codes, which will look something like:
AND pay_code IN (100, 105, 115, 125, 130)
The exact column name and surrounding SQL will vary between files.

4d. Add the new pay code in ascending numeric sequence. For example, if you are adding pay code 121 and the existing list reads 115, 125, the result should be 115, 121, 125. Do not alter any other part of the SQL.

4e. Update the Report Summary header. Near the top of the DataSet1 SQL you will find a comment block that looks like this:
-- Name:         [Report name]
-- Tab name:     [Tab name]
-- Version:      [e.g. 9.0]
-- Last updated: [Month Year]
-- Change ID:    [OSM number]

Update:
Version — increment to the next version (e.g. 9.0 becomes 10.0). All files in the suite must be incremented to the same version number.
Last updated — set to the current month and year (e.g. JUN 2026).
Change ID — enter the OSM Change ID obtained in Step 1.

4f. Save the file.

Step 5 — Test in the Preview Pane

Before deploying, use the report Preview pane in Visual Studio to test the changes:
1. Click the Preview tab on the report design surface.
2. Run the report.
3. Confirm no SQL syntax errors appear.
4. Confirm the report returns results.
5. Confirm the new pay code data appears in the output.

If there is a syntax error, check for missing commas, misplaced brackets, or incorrect pay code formatting. TSQL numeric values in IN() lists do not need single quotes.

Step 6 — Deploy to TEST

Follow the standard HR Reporting release and deployment procedure to deploy the updated .RDL files to the TEST environment. Refer to the how-to guide HOW TO - Manage Reports - Release and Deployment for the full deployment steps.

Step 7 — Tracy Validates in TEST

Notify Tracy that Version [N] is available in the TEST environment. Tracy should confirm:
1. The new pay code appears in the output of all affected reports.
2. No existing pay codes are missing from the output.
3. Report formatting is unchanged.

Do not proceed to LIVE until Tracy has confirmed all three criteria.

Step 8 — Deploy to LIVE

Once Tracy has signed off the TEST validation:

1. In Visual Studio, open the LIVE solution file from I:\OUIT\CoreHR Reports (separate .sln file from TEST).
2. For each updated .RDL file, right-click the appropriate folder in Solution Explorer and select Add > Existing Item.
3. Browse to the TEST solution folder and select the updated Version [N] .RDL file.
4. Follow the standard release and deployment procedure to deploy to LIVE.
5. Move the deployed files to the correct folder hierarchy within the LIVE environment.
6. Retire (remove or archive) the previous version .RDL files.

Step 9 — Confirm LIVE Output

Ask Tracy to confirm that the LIVE reports are returning the correct output with the new pay code visible. Once confirmed, the change is complete.

Step 10 — Close the Change Request

Update and close the OSM Change Request, noting the completion date and that testing was signed off by Tracy.

Back-Out Procedure

If a problem is found in LIVE after deployment:

1. Open the LIVE solution in Visual Studio.
2. Right-click the appropriate folder in Solution Explorer and select Add > Existing Item.
3. Browse to the TEST or QA solution and select the previous version (e.g. Version 9.0) .RDL file.
4. Deploy the previous version to LIVE using the standard release and deployment procedure.
5. Move the file to the correct folder hierarchy and remove the new version.
6. Ask Tracy to confirm LIVE has been restored to the previous state.
7. Raise a follow-up investigation before re-attempting the fix.

Rollback takes approximately 15 to 30 minutes. This change does not modify any data in PeopleXD — rollback does not result in any data loss.

Key Contacts

Tracy — validates and signs off report changes in TEST and LIVE.
Michael — confirms whether a pay code omission is a SQL issue or an Access Group configuration issue.
Marie Cooksey — Head of HR Systems, Business Owner / Approver on Change Requests.

t: HOW TO — Raise a Change Request for HR Reporting (OSM)
s: Guide to raising OSM Change Requests for HR Reporting SQL and report file changes at the University of Oxford. Covers the 14-section CR format, key fields, the CR template location, and how the OSM Change ID links back to the report files.
_text:
HOW TO — Raise a Change Request for HR Reporting (OSM)

What is OSM?

OSM (Oxford Service Management) is the University of Oxford's IT change control system. Any change to HR Reporting infrastructure — including SQL changes, report file edits, and configuration changes — must be recorded and approved via an OSM Change Request (CR) before work begins. This ensures a full audit trail and supports the university's change management governance requirements.

For HR Systems reporting changes, the Change Request is raised in PeopleXD's OSM module and follows a 14-section format.

When Do You Need a CR?

A Change Request is required before:
- Any edit to SQL within a .RDL report file
- Any change to a shared dataset or data source
- Deployment of updated report files to the TEST or LIVE environment
- Any configuration change to the HR Reporting environment

Raising a CR is always the first step — before any files are opened or edited.

The 14-Section CR Format

All Oxford HR Systems Change Requests use the following section structure. A blank template is available in the hris-change-requests GitHub repository at templates/change-request-template.md.

Section 1 — Details: What is changing? Describe the specific change being made, the files or systems affected, and the environment pipeline (TEST then LIVE).

Section 2 — Justification: Why is the change necessary? Describe the business reason, the problem being solved, and any deadlines or dependencies.

Section 3 — Related Changes: Are there any dependent changes that must happen at the same time or in a specific sequence? If none, state that explicitly.

Section 4 — Impact on Dependent Services: What is the impact on connected or downstream services? Who will be affected when the change is live?

Section 5 — Downtime: Will there be any service outage or at-risk period? If not, explain why not.

Section 6 — Effect of Not Applying: What happens if this change is not made? Describe the ongoing business impact of leaving the issue unresolved.

Section 7 — Risk Assessment: What could go wrong? How likely is it and how serious? What mitigations are in place?

Section 8 — Testing: Who will test the change and how? What criteria must be met before the change can be promoted to LIVE?

Section 9 — Implementation Plan: A numbered list of steps using the format: Step N — [action]. Owner: [name]. Each step should be on one line. Cover the end-to-end process from initial edit through to LIVE sign-off.

Section 10 — Communications Plan: Who needs to be informed and when? For minor internal reporting fixes, this is often minimal.

Section 11 — Business Owner / Approver: The person accountable for approving the change. For HR Systems reporting changes this is typically Marie Cooksey, Head of HR Systems.

Section 12 — Potential Security Impact: Does the change alter access controls, expose new data, or affect user permissions? Describe any security implications.

Section 13 — How Security Impact Will Be Tested: How will you confirm that no unintended access or data exposure has resulted from the change?

Section 14 — Back-Out Plan: A numbered list of steps to reverse the change if something goes wrong after deployment. Use the same Step N format as Section 9. Include an estimate of how long rollback will take and confirm whether rollback results in any data loss.

Key OSM Fields

When submitting the CR in OSM, two fields that are commonly confused:

Category — the type of item being changed. Common values: Report, Software, Data Fix, Configuration, Document, Enhancement, Patch. For changes to .RDL report files, use Report.

Justification / Type — the reason for the change. Common values: Bug Fix, Enhancement, Upgrade, Patch. For correcting a missing pay code or similar SQL omission, use Bug Fix.

These are separate fields. A typical HR reporting CR will have Category = Report and Justification = Bug Fix.

The Change ID

When OSM assigns a Change ID (the CR reference number), note it immediately. This number must be entered into the Report Summary comment block at the top of the DataSet1 SQL in each affected .RDL file. The format is:

-- Change ID:    [OSM number]

This ensures every deployed report file is traceable back to its authorising Change Request.

CR Template and Completed CRs

The blank CR template is held in the hris-change-requests GitHub repository:
hris-change-requests/templates/change-request-template.md

Completed CRs are stored in:
hris-change-requests/CRs/

Naming convention for CR files: CR-YYYY-MM-DD-short-description.md (kebab-case, lowercase, date = date drafted).

Example: CR-2026-06-18-pay-code-121-hr-report-suite.md

Guidelines for Completing the CR

Never invent information. If you do not know a value, use [TBC] or mark it for confirmation.
Always confirm Section 11 (Business Owner / Approver) before finalising.
Use British English throughout.
Implementation Plan steps should be concise and action-oriented — one step per line.
Back-Out Plan must always be included, even for low-risk changes.
Do not include information in the Description that belongs in Actions, or vice versa — keep background in Description and dated actions in the action log.

t: HOW TO: Create a Non-Payroll Company & Link the Org Hierarchy — Colleges & Halls UOXU
s: Step-by-step guide to setting up a non-payroll organisation structure in PeopleXD UOXU for Colleges & Halls (Company 90). Covers company creation, pay group (ZZ Do Not Use College Non-Pay), Pay Group Access, Data Centre, hierarchy reference data (Division 901, ZSD901, Z90101, Z901, Z902), Pay Administered By data migration (40 college codes, USER5), hierarchy linking via Portal, and linking Pay Administered By to each department (Step 7B). Includes screenshots from 12 June 2026 session with The Access Group.

HOW TO: Create a Non-Payroll Company
& Link the Org Hierarchy

Colleges & Halls — PeopleXD UOXU (Company 90)

System — PeopleXD (UOXU)

Topic — System Admin

Status — DRAFT — live UOXU screenshots embedded; pending screenshots noted

Version — 1.0 — 15 June 2026

Source — PeopleXD configuration session, 12 June 2026 (Conor, The Access Group)

Business Owner — Marie Cooksey, Head of HR Systems

Purpose

This guide explains how to set up a new non-payroll organisation structure in PeopleXD for a population that needs HR management (posts, appointments, hierarchy) but is not processed through payroll. Written for Colleges & Halls (Company 90) — steps apply to any non-payroll company.

Prerequisites

Payroll Administration access in PeopleXD

HR Administration access in PeopleXD

Agreed company code, hierarchy codes and naming conventions confirmed

Department records already exist in the system

Step 1 — Create the Non-Payroll Company

Navigation: Payroll Dashboard → Settings → Organisations

Organisations screen — Payroll Dashboard → Settings → Organisations

Select Copy Company

Choose the source company — Colleges and Halls

Source company — Colleges and Halls selected as the template to copy from

Enter new company code: 90

Rename the organisation: Non Payroll COLLEGES AND HALLS

Company 90 — code and name entered before saving

In the Contact field enter: REF2029 (internal reference)

Company 90 completed — Contact = REF2029, ready to review sections

Select Detail → review each section tab (Payroll Parameters, Payroll Calendar, Miscellaneous Parameters, Bonus Parameters)

Reviewing copied sections — Payroll Calendar highlighted; remove or clear any payroll-specific values not applicable to a non-payroll company

Remove all payroll-specific fields — revenue details, tax registration fields (Revenue Details section)

Leave payroll registration fields blank — this company will not run payroll; no calendar link needed. System may warn about missing calendar — expected and acceptable

Save

Note: If this company needs to become a registered payroll company in future, return and populate the tax, calendar and revenue fields at that point.

✓ Validate: Code 90 · Name = Non Payroll COLLEGES AND HALLS · Contact = REF2029 · No payroll registration details · Saves successfully

Step 2 — Create the Non-Payroll Pay Group

Navigation: Payroll Dashboard → Settings → Pay Groups

Pay Groups list — existing pay groups shown in dropdown; Non Employees is the source to duplicate

Locate the existing Non Employees pay group

Non Employees pay group (code 00) selected — note the University of Oxford company reference

Selecting Non Employees from the dropdown as the source for duplication

Select Duplicate

Change Pay Group Code to: 90

Change Pay Group Name to: ZZ Do Not Use College Non-Pay (ZZ prefix keeps it at the bottom of all lists — reduces risk of accidental assignment to a real employee)

Link to Company 90 in the Company Reference field

Duplicate pay group form — Pay Group 90 being configured with University Monthly copied settings; update code, name and company reference

Bottom of the pay group form — review fields and Save

Save

Known issue: Pay Group 90 failed to appear after creation during the 12 June session. This is a system issue — contact The Access Group via PXD Portal. Do not attempt to diagnose yourself. Do not delete the pay group if any staff have already been assigned to it.

✓ Validate: Pay Group Code = 90 · Linked to Company 90 · Appears in managed payroll list

Step 3 — Grant Pay Group Access

Navigation: Payroll Dashboard → Pay Group Access

Pay Group Access — existing user/pay group access list; use Add Pay Group to grant access to Pay Group 90

Select Add Pay Group (top right)

Add Pay Group Access dialog — enter username, select Pay Group 90, set All Input Locations

Enter the username of each user who needs visibility of Colleges & Halls salary data

Select Pay Group: 90 — ZZ Do Not Use College Non-Pay

Input Location: All Input Locations

Click OK

Repeat for all relevant users

Pay Group Access list filtered to confirm — ZZ Do Not Use College Non-Pay (Pay Group 90) showing for Portal Admin

Critical: Without Pay Group 90 access a user CANNOT see the salary tab for any Colleges & Halls staff — even with full company-level HR access. Company access alone is not sufficient.

✓ Validate: Pay Group 90 in each relevant user's access list · Salary tab visible on a test Colleges & Halls staff record

Step 4 — Add Company to Data Centre

Navigation: Data Centre → search Company → Company Settings

Add Company 90 to the company list

Complete fields (name, RSI title) consistent with existing companies

Save

Critical: Without this step users lose visibility of posts and appointments under Company 90 even after Pay Group access is granted. Both steps 3 and 4 are required.

✓ Validate: Company 90 appears in Company Settings list · Relevant users can see posts and appointments

Step 5 — Create the Hierarchy Reference Data

All navigation is via Reference Data in system settings. Create each level in order before moving to the next.

5.1 Division

Field — Value

Code — 901

Description — Colleges and Halls

Company — 90

Staff Requests — Leave inactive — not required for this company

Reference Data → User Field 1 Types — Division codes. S011 = Colleges and Halls shown as an example of how Division codes appear in the system

✓ Validate: Division 901 appears against Company 90

5.2 Subdivision (USER_CODE1)

Field — Value

Code — ZSD901

Description — Colleges and Halls

Active — Yes

Screenshot pending: Subdivision ZSD901 in PeopleXD reference data — capture during live UOXU configuration

5.3 Level 4 (USER_CODE2)

Field — Value

Code — Z90101

Description — Colleges and Halls

Active — Yes

Screenshot pending: Level 4 Z90101 in PeopleXD reference data — capture during live UOXU configuration

5.4 Management Units

Create two entries:

Code — Description — Active

Z901 — Colleges & Halls — Yes

Z902 — Permanent Private Halls — Yes

Screenshot pending: Management Units Z901 and Z902 in PeopleXD reference data — capture during live UOXU configuration

Step 6 — Load Pay Administered By Reference Data

Use the Data Migration tool to load all 40 college codes at once rather than entering them individually.

Navigation: Data Migration → Templates

The hierarchy mapping spreadsheet — shows all levels (Subdivision, Level 4, Management Unit, Department, Pay Administered By). Use this as your reference when building the structure in Step 7B

Download the HR Reference template and the Helper file from Data Migration → Templates

Open the HR Reference template

HR Reference File — blank template. Four columns required: Reference Type | Reference Code | Description | Active Indicator

Prepare your file in pipe-delimited format with these four columns: Reference Type | Reference Code | Description | Active Indicator

Reference Type must be: USER5 (this is the code for Pay Administered By — must be exact)

Populate all 40 college codes (see table below)

Populated upload file — all 40 college codes entered in pipe-delimited format with USER5 reference type and REF2029 suffix in description

t: HOW TO: Troubleshoot — UDF Data Uploaded Successfully but Not Visible on Employee Records
s: Troubleshooting order for a UDF bulk upload that the Data Migration Tool reports as Complete/0 Failed but a colleague can't see on the live employee record: check the Employee Search Person Filter (Active/Dormant/Both) first — the most common false alarm — then the Data Labels "Active" checkbox on the UDF field itself. Also lists what NOT to assume is the cause (Security Required, CorePortal Display, the Data Migration Tool's own Public/Private job-record flag) and cross-links the Data Migration Tool and UDF Configuration guides.
_text:
HOW TO: Troubleshoot — UDF Data Uploaded Successfully but Not Visible on Employee Records

Common ways this gets reported: "I uploaded UDF data but can't see it." "The UDF upload was successful but the values aren't showing on the employee record." "Data Migration Tool shows Complete, 0 Failed, but my colleague can't see the UDF data / can't see the field / can't see the values." "UDF data uploaded, not visible, not showing, not displaying on the employee's record." If any of that matches what you're seeing, start at Step 1 below.

Scenario

The Data Migration Tool shows a UDF (User Defined Field) bulk upload as Complete, 0 Failed — every record processed cleanly, no failures, no errors. But a colleague or user reports they cannot see the uploaded UDF data, cannot see the values, cannot see the field on the live employee record — it's just not visible, not showing, not displaying. There is no error anywhere in the Data Migration Tool. This guide is the troubleshooting order to work through when uploaded UDF data can't be seen, confirmed against real Oxford PeopleXD live and UAT environments, 18-19 September 2026, after a case that took half a day to resolve because the two relevant guides (Data Migration Tool and UDF Configuration) don't cross-reference each other. Check these in order — most cases resolve at step 1.

Step 1 — Check the Employee Search "Person Filter" FIRST

Before assuming anything is wrong with the data or the UDF configuration, check who the colleague is actually searching for and how.

Navigation: People Management Dashboard > Employees > View > Employee Search screen.

This screen has a "Person Filter" dropdown with three options: Active, Dormant, Active and Dormant. It defaults to Active only.

If the colleague is searching for a specific employee who has left the organisation (a dormant record / leaver), that employee will not appear in the search results at all — regardless of whether the UDF data uploaded correctly. This is not a data problem or a configuration problem. It is a search-scope problem, and it is the single most common false alarm in this scenario.

Fix: change the Person Filter to "Active and Dormant" (or "Dormant") and search again. If the employee and their UDF data now appear, the upload was fine all along — nothing else in this guide needs checking.

Source: "People Management Dashboard" (Access Group Help Centre) section 2.4, and "Leavers" (Access Group Help Centre) — both confirm Employee Search defaults to Active-only via the Person Filter control.

Only move to Step 2 if the employee in question is confirmed Active (or the colleague is searching with "Active and Dormant" already selected) and the UDF value is still not visible.

Step 2 — Check the Data Labels "Active" checkbox on the UDF field itself

This is the real fix when Step 1 doesn't explain it — a genuine configuration setting on the UDF field, not a data problem. The Data Migration Tool's "Complete, 0 Failed" status only confirms the values were written to the database; it says nothing about whether the field is switched on to display.

Navigation: HR Admin Setup Settings > User Defined Objects > [select the Reference Code for the UDF] > row 3-dot menu > Data Labels.

Each individual data field/label on the UDF has its own "Active" checkbox. If this checkbox is unchecked, that field will not display on screen for ANY employee — active or dormant — even though the underlying data uploaded successfully and exists in the database. Unlike Step 1, this is not scoped to one employee; it hides the field for everyone.

This checkbox is also the de-facto delete mechanism for UDF list items — there is no separate "Delete" function; deactivating an item is how you remove it from display. So if a UDF item was recently edited, recreated, or the object rebuilt, it's easy for this checkbox to end up unchecked without anyone deliberately hiding it.

Fix: tick "Active" for the relevant field on the Data Labels screen and save. The already-uploaded values should now display without any re-upload.

Source: "PeopleXD People Management - User Defined Field Configuration V1.0.pdf", section 3.2 (Data Labels table: "Active — Select this to ensure the field displays on screen") and section 4.1.2, "Edit an Existing UDF Item" ("Update the Active indicator to show / hide a field"). Confirmed identical wording in both the How To Guides copy and the Access Group Help Centre copy of this guide.

Things ruled out today — do not assume these are the cause without evidence

These three were checked and eliminated during the 18-19 September 2026 case. Each gates something different from "can a colleague see this on the employee record" — don't burn time on them again without a specific reason to suspect one:

- "Security Required" toggle (UDF Advanced screen). This gates the HR administrator's OWN access to the UDF record via People Management. It does not affect what any other colleague sees, and it is explicitly not applicable to manager/employee CorePortal access either (source doc, section 6, closing note, verbatim). Not the cause of "my colleague can't see it."

- CorePortal Display / Hide Dates toggle (UDF Advanced screen, "CorePortal" section). This gates Employee/Manager Self-Service (ESS/MSS) visibility only — the employee's own portal view, not an internal admin's People Management screen. If the colleague who can't see the data is another HR administrator (not the employee via self-service), this toggle is irrelevant.

- The "Private/Public" flag on the Data Migration Tool's own upload record (3-dot menu on the migration job in the Data Migration Templates/Options list). This gates visibility of the MIGRATION JOB record itself within the Data Migration Tool's own list of past uploads — i.e. whether another admin can see that the upload happened. It has no effect on whether the uploaded data displays on the employee's actual record. Do not confuse "can another admin see this upload job in the tool" with "can a colleague see this field on the employee record" — they are unrelated settings on unrelated screens.

Why this took half a day: the documentation gap

The Data Migration Tool guide documents the upload mechanism and warns that the target UDF object must already exist/be configured before upload — but says nothing about post-upload display. The UDF Configuration guide documents the Person Filter and Data Labels Active checkbox — but isn't linked from the Data Migration Tool guide, so someone following the upload process has no signpost to the display-side settings when the upload itself reports success. There was previously no single document connecting "upload completed with 0 failures" to "why can't it be seen" — this guide is that connection. See also the Data Migration Tool User Guide (upload procedure, prerequisite that the UDF object must exist first) and the UDF Configuration guide (Person Filter, Data Labels Active checkbox, Security Required, CorePortal Advanced options) — read together, in that order, for the full upload-to-display picture.

Quick reference — troubleshooting order

1. Person Filter on Employee Search — is the employee Active or Dormant? (most common cause)
2. Data Labels "Active" checkbox on the specific UDF field — is it ticked?
3. Only if 1 and 2 don't explain it, and only with a specific reason to suspect it: Security Required (admin's own access only) or CorePortal Display (ESS/MSS only) — neither explains one colleague not seeing data on People Management.
4. The Data Migration Tool's own Public/Private flag on the upload job record is unrelated to any of the above — it only affects visibility of the migration job itself in the tool's history list.
